samples.text:
Nowadays, many people suffer from health problems such as obesity and heart disease. Some people believe that everyone should take care of their own health, but others think the government should play an important role to encourage healthy lifestyle. In my opinion, both individuals and governments has responsibility, but the government role is very important.

On the one hand, it is true that people should be responsible for their own health. Adults can decide what they eat, how much they exercise and whether they smoke or not. Nobody can force another person to go to the gym or eat vegetables. If someone chooses an unhealthy lifestyle, it is their own decision and they should accept the results. Also, some people do not like when the government tells them how to live.

On the other hand, the government can help people a lot. Many people do not know enough about healthy food, so government can run campaigns on TV and in schools to educate them. In addition, the government can put higher taxes on cigarettes and sugary drinks, which make these products less attractive. It can also build parks and sports centres so people have more chance to do exercise. When people are healthier, the country spend less money on hospitals.

In my view, individuals must make the final choice, but government should make the healthy choice easier. For example, if fruit and vegetables are cheap and there are safe places for cycling, more people will live healthily.

To conclude, personal responsibility is important, but governments also need to play a major role. Working together, they can help people to live longer and more healthy lives.

samples.text:
Rising rates of lifestyle-related illnesses such as diabetes and heart disease have raised the question of who should be responsible for people's health. Some believe this is a matter of personal choice, while others argue that governments should take an active role in promoting healthy living. I believe that although individuals must take responsibility for their choices, governments have an important part to play in shaping those choices.

Those who emphasise individual responsibility argue that adults have the right to decide how they live. Eating habits, exercise and smoking are personal decisions, and many people resent being told what to do by the state. In addition, when people take ownership of their health, they are more likely to maintain positive habits over time than if they are simply following official advice. From this perspective, government campaigns can seem patronising and a waste of public money.

However, there are strong reasons for governments to intervene. Individual choices are heavily influenced by the environment people live in. Unhealthy food is often cheaper and more heavily advertised than healthier options, and many neighbourhoods lack safe spaces for walking or cycling. Governments can address these issues through measures such as taxes on sugary drinks, clear food labelling and investment in parks and sports facilities. Moreover, since poor health places enormous pressure on public healthcare systems, the state has a legitimate interest in prevention.

In my view, the most effective approach combine both perspectives. People should remain free to make their own decisions, but governments should make healthy options easier, cheaper and more attractive, so that the responsible choice is also the convenient one.

In conclusion, while individuals are ultimately responsible for how they live, I believe governments should play a major role in encouraging healthier lifestyles, as this benefits both citizens and society as a whole.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant examples · logical organisation and good range of linking · less common vocabulary (patronising, food labelling) · frequent error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Few would dispute that good health depends heavily on everyday behaviour, yet there is considerable disagreement about who should take responsibility for it. Some maintain that health is essentially a personal matter, whereas others believe governments should actively encourage citizens to lead healthier lives. In my view, individual responsibility and state involvement are not mutually exclusive, and the latter is often necessary for the former to be meaningful.

The argument for personal responsibility rests on the principle of autonomy. Adults are entitled to make decisions about their own diet, activity levels and habits, even when those decisions carry risks, and government intervention in such matters can easily become paternalistic. There is also a practical point: lasting change in behaviour tends to come from personal motivation rather than external pressure, so public campaigns may achieve little if people are not genuinely committed to improving their health.

Nevertheless, this view underestimates how strongly circumstances shape behaviour. People on low incomes may find nutritious food less affordable and less accessible than processed alternatives, while those living in areas without parks or safe streets have fewer opportunities to exercise. Commercial pressures, such as the aggressive marketing of high-sugar products to children, further tilt the balance towards unhealthy choices. Governments are uniquely placed to counteract these influences through regulation, taxation, urban planning and education. Furthermore, because the cost of treating preventable illness is largely borne by taxpayers, the state has a clear interest in reducing it.

For these reasons, I believe governments should play a major role, not by dictating how people live, but by creating conditions in which healthy choices are realistic for everyone. Individuals would still be responsible for their decisions, but they would make them in an environment that supports rather than undermines their wellbeing.

In conclusion, while personal responsibility remains important, it cannot be exercised equally when circumstances differ so widely. Active government involvement is therefore essential to enabling people to lead healthier lives.
samples.why: Both views fully examined with well-supported reasoning · nuanced, clearly argued position · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (paternalistic, autonomy) · wide range of accurate complex structures.
